analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax and locks in a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 222 cosponsors — 215 Republicans and 7 Democrats — but was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal estate tax — the tax owed when a person's estate passes to heirs — permanently, and also repeal the tax on transfers that skip a generation. It would lock in a 35% gift tax rate and a $5 million lifetime exemption for gifts. It never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. Under current law, only a small fraction of the very largest estates owes any estate tax at all, so repeal is a direct tax cut concentrated almost entirely among families with multi-million- and billion-dollar fortunes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently ends the estate tax for anyone dying after enactment, so no estate would ever owe it again.
It permanently ends the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth is passed directly to grandchildren, allowing such transfers tax-free.
It locks in a 35% maximum gift tax rate and a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption, letting wealthy individuals shift large sums to heirs during life at low tax cost.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises revenue from the largest fortunes; repealing it means that revenue has to be replaced by borrowing or by other taxes, which fall on everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes a tax paid only by the very largest estates, shifting the revenue burden to other taxpayers or to future debt.
The bill locks in a $5 million lifetime gift exemption permanently, which is worth most to households wealthy enough to give away millions while living.
Supporters argued the estate tax forces heirs to sell farms and small businesses, but only estates above the large exemption thresholds owe the tax at all, so any relief is highly concentrated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers. There is no meaningful offsetting benefit to ordinary working people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Kevin Brady introduced the bill on March 30, 2011.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
That was the last action ever taken on the bill; the committee scheduled no hearing or markup and the full House never voted.
Despite 222 cosponsors — 215 of them Republicans, giving the bill more than enough votes to pass the House if it had been brought up — no vote ever occurred.
Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off, since the estate tax on the largest fortunes remained in force rather than being repealed; families with very large estates, and the estate-planning industry that serves them, lost the chance at a permanent tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers kept the estate tax

for.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, generation-skipping transfer, and gift taxes permanently.

for.name: 215 of 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 215 of its 222 total cosponsors.

for.name: 7 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, providing the small share of bipartisan support it had.

against.name: Chair Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, keeping it from reaching the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 215 of the bill's 222 cosponsors were House Republicans, with only 7 Democrats signing on.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the only federal tax owed on the largest intergenerational fortunes, a direct windfall to a few thousand families each year whose cost is spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and trust services (law firms, wealth advisors)
industries.note: Permanent repeal would end much of the estate-tax planning business that large fortunes generate, while the locked-in $5 million lifetime gift exemption would keep lucrative gifting and trust work alive.
